title: Survival curves: show who remains at risk after each event
summary: Build a step curve from observed events, keep censoring visible and stop trusting a thin tail.
body:
Build a step curve from observed events, keep censoring visible and stop trusting a thin tail.

Define the event and the clock

A survival curve estimates the share of a starting cohort that has not yet experienced a specified event by elapsed time. A device-failure chart, for instance, needs a clear start such as commissioning and an event such as first unrecoverable shutdown. Mixing calendar dates with elapsed operating days changes the risk set. Units matter too: a device observed for 47 calendar days but active for 31 operating days is not interchangeable with one observed continuously. Event-aligned time series can show measurements around a milestone, while a survival curve asks when the first event occurs. Decide how replacement devices, repeat failures and delayed entry will be treated before fitting the curve; the simple right-censored calculation below assumes every device enters at elapsed time zero.

A censor mark is not a failure

Right censoring means observation ended without the event being seen. A study cutoff, withdrawal or lost sensor feed can create one, but those reasons need separate counts because their relationship to failure risk may differ. The Kaplan–Meier step drops only when events occur. A censor at time 59 leaves the height unchanged while reducing the group available for later event times. When events and censors share a recorded time, declare whether events are processed before same-time censors; the code uses that convention. Put the censor marks on the curve and provide an at-risk table at chosen time ticks. Missing periods are a different data problem: do not silently turn an unobserved failure time into a clean censor without checking what was actually known.

Read the tail against its denominator

A flat tail can look reassuring even when only two devices remain under observation. Show the number at risk at regular, meaningful intervals and consider ending the displayed curve where support becomes too sparse for the decision. Do not stretch the last estimated step into a guarantee beyond follow-up. If two cohorts enter in different years or face different servicing policies, their curves are descriptive until the cohort definitions and confounding are reviewed. Small-sample uncertainty belongs beside the estimate, and a confidence band needs a stated method. An ordinary percent-without-failure line is not equivalent when follow-up lengths differ because it treats early withdrawals as though they had complete observation.

Keep the underlying event ledger

The plot is a compression of the event ledger, not a substitute for it. Preserve device ID, entry time, exit time, event flag, censor reason, cohort, and data-cutoff date. Reconcile the at-risk count before each event: prior risk minus prior events and censors must equal the next risk count. If failures can be precluded by a different event, a conventional one-event survival curve may answer the wrong question; define a competing-event analysis instead. Empirical CDFs are useful when event times are fully observed, but they do not automatically handle censoring. Export a table of each step time, event count, censor count, risk count and estimated survival so a reader can audit every drop without estimating coordinates from pixels.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import isfinite

def device_survival_steps(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]]):
    identifiers = [device_id for device_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("device IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(duration) or duration < 0 or type(failed) is not bool
           for _, duration, failed in records):
        raise ValueError("duration and event flags must be valid")
    events = Counter(duration for _, duration, failed in records if failed)
    censors = Counter(duration for _, duration, failed in records if not failed)
    risk_count, survival, steps = len(records), 1.0, []
    for duration in sorted(events.keys() | censors.keys()):
        failed_count = events[duration]
        censored_count = censors[duration]
        survival *= 1 - failed_count / risk_count
        steps.append((duration, risk_count, failed_count,
                      censored_count, survival))
        risk_count -= failed_count + censored_count
    return steps

depot_devices = [
    ("station-47", 3, True), ("station-59", 4, False),
    ("station-83", 4, True), ("station-97", 7, False),
]
depot_steps = device_survival_steps(depot_devices)
assert depot_steps[0] == (3, 4, 1, 0, 0.75)
assert depot_steps[1] == (4, 3, 1, 1, 0.5)
assert depot_steps[-1][-1] == 0.5

Performance and operating cost

Counting and sorting N event or censor records takes O(N log N) time and O(N) space. The function returns every observed exit time so censors can be marked even when the step height stays level. It assumes entry at time zero, one terminal event, and a declared event-before-censor tie rule; it does not calculate confidence limits or correct informative censoring. Validate the event ledger and at-risk table before drawing smooth-looking output.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a censored record as an observed failure or as complete follow-up.
  • Omitting at-risk counts while interpreting the last flat segment.
  • Combining elapsed operating time with calendar time on one axis.
  • Comparing cohorts without checking different entry policies, follow-up windows or censor reasons.

Validation drill

Audit 47 devices across two installation cohorts. Print the risk set at months 0, 6, 12 and 18, mark withdrawals, then explain where the tail no longer supports a useful comparison.

title: Mosaic plots: make cell area match the underlying count
summary: Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.
body:
Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.

Choose a denominator before drawing tiles

A two-way mosaic plot partitions one rectangle by a contingency table. Each first-category column gets width proportional to its count in the full data set. Within that column, second-category tile heights represent conditional shares. Multiplying width by height yields the cell's share of the grand total. That area contract is the point of the chart. If the column widths are all equal instead, the display answers a different question: it emphasizes within-group composition and conceals unequal group sizes. Stacked bars are often easier to read when exact conditional rates are the primary comparison, while treemaps use area for hierarchical totals rather than a two-way cross-classification.

Declare the table grain

Count one unit only once in the table unless the chart explicitly represents events rather than entities. If a shipment can appear in several outcome categories, a standard contingency table is not valid until a mutually exclusive rule is chosen. A missing outcome is its own category or an explicit exclusion; quietly dropping it changes every tile's area. Aggregation grain and denominator should be fixed upstream. Record the category order even if one group has a zero count, and distinguish a true zero cell from a category never collected. Reconcile each column subtotal with source records before calculating widths, then reconcile all columns to the grand total. A plot that looks rectangular can still be numerically wrong.

Read association without mistaking size for rate

A wider group contributes more observations, while a taller tile within that group represents a larger conditional share. Readers often compare tile heights across groups and forget the width, or compare areas when the question is only about rates. Label both count and within-group percentage in a companion table. If a tiny tile cannot hold text, put the label outside or leave it to an accessible table rather than enlarging the tile. Heatmaps can encode a rate in color, but their equal-size cells do not show count automatically. Do not imply statistical significance from a striking mosaic pattern; sampling design, uncertainty and multiple subgroup inspections remain separate questions.

Keep order and coverage stable

A mosaic is more legible with a limited number of well-defined categories. Many thin columns or slivers make the visual fragile on phones and at high zoom. Sort categories by a declared business order, not by whichever tile creates the strongest pattern in each filter state. If a dashboard filter removes units, recompute column totals and display the new grand total; a stale denominator can make area and labels disagree. Linked filters should expose which cohort is selected. Export the exact cross-tabulation with count, row total, grand total, conditional percentage and excluded count so the visible geometry can be independently reconstructed.

Worked contract

def mosaic_tiles(table: dict[str, dict[str, int]],
                 outcomes: list[str]):
    if not table or not outcomes or len(outcomes) != len(set(outcomes)):
        raise ValueError("groups and ordered outcomes are required")
    if any(set(cells) != set(outcomes) for cells in table.values()):
        raise ValueError("every group needs every outcome, including zeros")
    if any(type(count) is not int or count < 0
           for cells in table.values() for count in cells.values()):
        raise ValueError("counts must be nonnegative integers")
    group_totals = {group: sum(cells.values()) for group, cells in table.items()}
    if any(total == 0 for total in group_totals.values()):
        raise ValueError("empty groups need a separate missing-data state")
    grand_total = sum(group_totals.values())
    tiles, left = [], 0.0
    for group, cells in table.items():
        right = left + group_totals[group] / grand_total
        bottom = 0.0
        for outcome in outcomes:
            top = bottom + cells[outcome] / group_totals[group]
            tiles.append((group, outcome, left, right, bottom, top,
                          cells[outcome]))
            bottom = top
        left = right
    return tiles

review_counts = {
    "early shift": {"accepted": 47, "returned": 13},
    "late shift": {"accepted": 20, "returned": 20},
}
review_tiles = mosaic_tiles(review_counts, ["accepted", "returned"])
early_accepted = review_tiles[0]
assert abs((early_accepted[3] - early_accepted[2]) *
           (early_accepted[5] - early_accepted[4]) - 0.47) < 1e-12
assert review_tiles[-1][-1] == 20

Performance and operating cost

For G groups and K outcome categories, validation and tile construction take O(GK) time and O(GK) output space. The positions are normalized to a unit square; the first tile covers 47 percent of the area because 47 of 100 reviewed shipments fall in that cell. Floating-point boundaries are drawing coordinates, not replacement counts. Keep the integer table available for labels and audit exports.

Common Mistakes

  • Making every group equally wide while claiming tile area represents total count.
  • Dropping unknown outcomes without updating the denominator and exclusion note.
  • Enlarging tiny tiles to fit labels, which breaks the area contract.
  • Reading an attractive pattern as evidence of association without examining uncertainty or sampling.

Validation drill

Cross-tabulate 83 inspected shipments by shift and disposition, including an unknown disposition. Reconcile the grand total and verify that each tile area equals its cell count divided by 83.

title: Ternary plots: preserve the total behind a three-part composition
summary: Map three nonnegative parts into a triangle only after defining what the whole contains.
body:
Map three nonnegative parts into a triangle only after defining what the whole contains.

The triangle represents a closed whole

A ternary plot places three nonnegative components of one whole at a point inside a triangle. A point near a corner has a large share of the component named at that corner. The chart requires a real closure rule: if raw materials, labor and transport make only 83 percent of a project budget, normalizing those three to 100 percent silently discards the remainder. Add a declared other category, change the question or use a different display. Stacked composition is easier when the reader needs several exact shares. A ternary plot earns its space when the trade-off among exactly three parts is itself the question and the total is comparable or available elsewhere.

Keep the raw total next to normalized shares

Closure removes scale. A project costing 47 units and another costing 470 can occupy the same triangle point when their ratios match. Preserve total cost as a table column, size encoding with a disclosed area scale, or a linked separate chart. Do not let marker color quietly reintroduce a fourth variable without a readable legend and accessible alternative. Area-scaled markers explain why marker radius is not proportional to magnitude. Zeros are legitimate triangle-edge cases, whereas negative components or a zero total cannot be mapped as shares. Before plotting, decide whether a recorded zero is a real absence, a rounded small positive amount or missing data; these cases should not share one symbol.

A trend can be a denominator effect

If one component's share rises, at least one other share must fall even when its raw amount is unchanged. That closure constraint can manufacture apparent negative relationships between parts. Compare raw components and totals before attributing a movement to a process change. Correlation heatmaps on closed shares need special care for exactly this reason. If several periods are shown, connect points only when each project ID and period order are stable. Label direction and elapsed time; a long geometric move is a large change in composition, not necessarily a large change in dollars or units. The triangle should not be used as a causal diagram.

Fix corners, orientation and precision

Choose a component order and corner labeling once for every panel and export. Reordering corners rotates the apparent story even when the numbers are unchanged. Use meaningful tick spacing and consistent normalization, preferably with a table reporting the original values and resulting shares to a stated precision. When values are rounded, their displayed shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1; keep full precision for coordinates and explain display rounding. Parallel coordinates offer another way to inspect several components without enforcing a three-part closure. For accessible interaction, keyboard focus should reveal all three components, the raw total and the record ID, not just an unlabeled point location.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def triangle_positions(records: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]):
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("composition IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    points = []
    for record_id, materials, labor, transport in records:
        parts = (materials, labor, transport)
        if any(not isfinite(part) or part < 0 for part in parts):
            raise ValueError("components must be finite and nonnegative")
        total = sum(parts)
        if total <= 0:
            raise ValueError("a zero total has no composition")
        x_position = (labor + transport / 2) / total
        y_position = (sqrt(3) / 2) * transport / total
        points.append((record_id, x_position, y_position, total,
                       tuple(part / total for part in parts)))
    return points

budget_points = triangle_positions([
    ("depot-47", 47, 31, 22),
    ("depot-59", 94, 62, 44),
])
assert abs(budget_points[0][1] - 0.42) < 1e-12
assert budget_points[0][1:3] == budget_points[1][1:3]
assert budget_points[0][3] == 100
assert budget_points[1][3] == 200

Performance and operating cost

Validating and normalizing N compositions costs O(N) time and O(N) output space. The two budgets share coordinates because their proportions match, yet their totals differ by a factor of two. The function supplies plotting coordinates for corners materials-left, labor-right and transport-top; it does not determine whether the three categories truly exhaust the business total. That semantic check belongs at the data boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Normalizing an incomplete three-part subset without naming the omitted share.
  • Comparing triangle distance as though it represented absolute amount.
  • Treating closure-induced negative relationships as independent evidence.
  • Changing corner order between panels or hiding raw totals after normalization.

Validation drill

Plot 59 project budgets using three exhaustive cost components. Identify any zero-total or negative record, retain the raw totals and explain why two projects with identical shares can require different spending decisions.

title: CUSUM charts: accumulate small departures from a stable target
summary: Define the reference process, update rule and alert threshold before reading a rising trace.
body:
Define the reference process, update rule and alert threshold before reading a rising trace.

A cumulative trace needs a frozen baseline

A cumulative-sum chart can detect a sustained small departure that a point-by-point threshold misses. Start with a process metric measured at consistent intervals and a target estimated from an independent, stable baseline period. A cumulative sum of raw values will drift simply because the metric is positive; subtract the target and a reference allowance before accumulating evidence of an upward shift. Use a separate lower trace for downward shifts. P charts handle varying binomial denominators; their rate and limits should not be replaced by a CUSUM of unadjusted percentages. If observation precision or exposure changes across periods, standardize or model that change before applying a fixed CUSUM rule.

The allowance and threshold are design choices

In a tabular upper CUSUM, each new value adds its deviation from the target minus an allowance, and negative running totals reset to zero. A lower CUSUM mirrors the logic for downward movement. The allowance controls the size of shift the chart is tuned to notice; the decision threshold controls when an alert is raised. Neither number is a universal constant. Calibrate them against the operational false-alarm rate and detection delay the team can tolerate, using an appropriate baseline model. Uncertainty displays help explain how noisy short runs can be. The worked numbers below demonstrate mechanics only and must not be copied as an alert policy for another process.

A signal is a review trigger

Mark the exact first threshold crossing on the chart. Keep every earlier point and the zero resets visible; truncating the history can make the signal look instantaneous. An alert says the observed sequence is unusual under the chosen reference model, not that a particular maintenance event caused it. Event annotations need timestamps and a caution about causal interpretation. If a baseline is re-estimated after every signal, the chart can absorb the very drift it was intended to detect. Version the target, allowance, threshold and any planned reset date. When a legitimate process change establishes a new operating state, start a documented new chart rather than silently splicing scales.

Audit the measurement pipeline

A sustained run of delayed, duplicated or missing readings can resemble a process shift. Validate sampling cadence, units, sensor identity and data revision status before interpreting the trace. Time-series gaps must remain gaps or be handled by an explicit rule; inserting zero will push a lower trace down for the wrong reason. Serial correlation also changes the false-alarm behavior of a rule calibrated for independent observations. Keep an export with period ID, raw reading, target version, upper and lower cumulative values, and alert state. Chart manifests make the calculation reproducible after a dashboard or threshold update.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def process_shift_trace(readings: list[float], target: float,
                        allowance: float, threshold: float):
    if (not all(isfinite(value) for value in [*readings, target,
                                               allowance, threshold])
            or allowance < 0 or threshold <= 0):
        raise ValueError("finite readings, nonnegative allowance and positive threshold required")
    upper = lower = 0.0
    trace = []
    for period_index, reading in enumerate(readings, start=1):
        upper = max(0.0, upper + reading - target - allowance)
        lower = max(0.0, lower + target - reading - allowance)
        trace.append((period_index, upper, lower,
                      upper >= threshold, lower >= threshold))
    return trace

depot_trace = process_shift_trace([48, 49, 52, 54],
                                  target=47, allowance=2, threshold=8)
assert depot_trace[:2] == [(1, 0.0, 0.0, False, False),
                           (2, 0.0, 0.0, False, False)]
assert depot_trace[-1] == (4, 8.0, 0.0, True, False)

Performance and operating cost

Updating N readings takes O(N) time and O(N) space when the full trace is retained; an online alarm needs O(1) state. The sequence reaches the illustrative upper threshold only after two larger readings accumulate. No false-alarm guarantee follows from those values. Choose target, allowance and threshold from the real measurement process and validate assumptions such as independence or expected exposure before production alerts.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a target recomputed from the same drifting window being monitored.
  • Copying example allowance and threshold values into a live alert without calibration.
  • Filling missing readings with zero or treating duplicate periods as independent evidence.
  • Calling the first alert proof of a specific cause rather than a trigger for investigation.

Validation drill

Monitor 47 daily throughput readings. Freeze a baseline version, compare an upper and lower trace, record every reset, and test how one missing day changes the alert when it is omitted versus incorrectly filled with zero.

title: Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
summary: Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.
body:
Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.

Event time is not calendar time

An event-aligned chart puts each subject's event at relative time zero. This lets a reader compare trajectories before and after events that occurred on different calendar dates. Store the actual event timestamp as well as the relative offset; otherwise seasonality, outages and policy changes disappear. Specify whether an offset means elapsed hours, calendar days or complete reporting periods. Time-series period rules are essential when the event occurs late in a day or across a daylight-saving change.

Fix the baseline rule

A common display subtracts each subject's pre-event value or divides by it. These produce different shapes and units. Select the baseline window before inspecting outcomes, report how many valid observations contributed to it, and reject a percentage change when the baseline is zero. If one subject has only one pre-event measurement and another has 47, their aligned curves carry different reliability. Denominator and grain rules should stay visible with the chart. Plot absolute values alongside normalized values when the magnitude of the original series matters.

Missing is not flat

Do not fill missing pre-event days with the baseline or connect a line across an unobserved outage without a marker. A cohort average at relative day five may use fewer subjects than at day one because follow-up ends; show the contributing count by offset. Attrition can make a trend look like improvement. Small-sample uncertainty belongs near sparse tails, and forecast intervals must not be substituted for missing actual observations.

The line does not prove an effect

A change at time zero can reflect selection into the event, a concurrent intervention, regression to the mean or ordinary seasonality. An annotation identifies timing, not causality. Compare a relevant untreated group or a pre-specified benchmark if the decision requires an effect estimate, and state the assumptions of that comparison. Annotation and causal-claim boundaries apply here. Export subject ID, event date, relative offset, original value, baseline window, normalized value and eligibility state so every plotted line can be reconstructed.

Worked contract

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite

def event_aligned_change(event_day: date, observations: dict[date, float],
                         baseline_days: tuple[date, ...]
                        ) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    if not baseline_days or len(set(baseline_days)) != len(baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline days must be distinct")
    if any(day >= event_day or day not in observations for day in baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline must be observed before the event")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in observations.values()):
        raise ValueError("observations must be finite")
    baseline = sum(observations[day] for day in baseline_days) / len(baseline_days)
    return sorted(((day - event_day).days, value, value - baseline)
                  for day, value in observations.items())

incident_counts = {
    date(2026, 10, 5): 47, date(2026, 10, 6): 59,
    date(2026, 10, 8): 38, date(2026, 10, 9): 35,
}
aligned = event_aligned_change(
    date(2026, 10, 7), incident_counts,
    (date(2026, 10, 5), date(2026, 10, 6)),
)
assert aligned == [(-2, 47, -6), (-1, 59, 6), (1, 38, -15), (2, 35, -18)]
assert all(offset != 0 for offset, _, _ in aligned)

Performance and operating cost

For N observations and B baseline days, validation and averaging take O(N+B) time; sorting relative periods takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. The function leaves missing event day zero absent instead of inventing a value. Calendar dates are appropriate only when day-level reporting is the contract; intraday events need zoned timestamps and a declared binning method. Subtracting a baseline describes change, not a causal estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Discarding calendar dates after alignment and losing concurrent-event context.
  • Choosing a favorable baseline window after seeing the result.
  • Drawing a continuous line over days with no observations.
  • Calling a post-event change proof that the event caused it.

Validation drill

Align 81 facilities around a maintenance intervention. Show each facility's baseline window and post-event coverage, then recompute the cohort curve using only facilities observed through day 14.

title: Empirical CDFs: read thresholds and tails without choosing bins
summary: Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.
body:
Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.

The step answers a threshold question

An empirical cumulative distribution function, or ECDF, gives the fraction of observed values less than or equal to each threshold. A point at 47 minutes and 0.8 means 80 percent of observations took at most 47 minutes. Unlike a histogram, it needs no bin width, so comparisons across groups are less sensitive to display choices. It still depends on the population, missing-value policy and observation window. Distribution plots should expose those rules before any percentile is interpreted.

Ties produce one jump

Repeated measurements at the same value create one larger step. If 31 of 81 jobs finish at exactly 12 minutes, the ECDF rises by 31/81 there; do not create a fake continuous slope between identical values. To compute a nearest-rank percentile, choose the first observed value whose cumulative share meets or exceeds the requested probability. Other quantile conventions interpolate and can return a number no job achieved. State the convention, especially for service targets. Sampling rules determine whether a percentile describes all jobs or a selected frame.

Keep the tail visible

Most observations can cluster near a short duration while a few long delays drive customer pain. An ECDF makes the proportion under a service threshold easy to read, but the far-right tail may still be squeezed by the axis. Add an inset, tail table or direct threshold counts when the rare cases matter. A survival-style complementary curve, one minus the ECDF, answers what fraction exceeds a threshold; be clear about strict versus inclusive inequalities at ties. Small samples need counts beside smooth-looking curves.

Compare only compatible cohorts

Two curves can differ because of case mix, eligibility, time window or measurement precision. Use consistent axis limits and units, label sample sizes, and show whether pending cases were excluded or censored. A naive ECDF of only completed jobs makes the slow unfinished work disappear. For a queue with unresolved jobs, use an analysis that handles censoring or restrict the claim to completed jobs. Observation status is part of the underlying data, not a cosmetic legend choice.

Worked contract

from math import ceil, isfinite

def completion_ecdf(minutes: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, int, float]]:
    if not minutes or any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in minutes):
        raise ValueError("need finite nonnegative durations")
    ordered = sorted(minutes)
    steps = []
    for value in ordered:
        if steps and steps[-1][0] == value:
            steps[-1] = (value, steps[-1][1] + 1, 0.0)
        else:
            steps.append((value, 1, 0.0))
    cumulative = 0
    result = []
    for value, tied, _ in steps:
        cumulative += tied
        result.append((value, tied, cumulative / len(ordered)))
    return result

durations = [12, 12, 31, 47, 81]
curve = completion_ecdf(durations)
nearest_rank_80 = sorted(durations)[ceil(0.8 * len(durations)) - 1]
assert curve[0] == (12, 2, 0.4)
assert curve[-1][2] == 1.0 and nearest_rank_80 == 47

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N durations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space for the ordered copy and output; scanning ties is O(N). Already-sorted warehouse output avoids the local sort. A chart with many distinct observations may still need visual reduction at screen resolution, but threshold queries should use the exact ordered values. The simple ECDF treats every supplied duration as complete and equally weighted; it is not a censored-data estimator.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a completed-only ECDF as the distribution of all started jobs.
  • Treating a large jump at a tied value as a renderer defect.
  • Quoting a percentile without its sample size and quantile convention.
  • Moving axis bounds between cohorts and comparing apparent steepness.

Validation drill

Build curves for two depot cohorts of 47 and 81 completed cases. Include repeated durations and unresolved work, then report the fraction within 31 minutes and exactly which cases were excluded.

title: Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
summary: Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.
body:
Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.

A stack has two possible questions

An absolute stacked bar shows a total and its parts in the same unit. A normalized bar forces every total to one and shows the mix instead. These are not interchangeable. If depot A closes 47 of 81 requests while depot B closes 470 of 810, both have the same closed share, but the latter carries ten times the workload. Place total and share in adjacent views when both matter. Define the denominator before calculating either bar. The title should say whether the horizontal extent means requests or a fraction of eligible requests.

Keep categories stable

Assign each status one color and one position across periods. If a status disappears, retain its zero-valued place in the data contract rather than shifting every later segment. The unanchored middle segments in a stack are difficult to compare precisely; when one category is the focus, use a grouped bar or a separate trend. Sort bars by a declared metric, such as eligible volume, and keep that order fixed across comparison panels. Facet ordering follows the same rule.

Handle absent and ineligible records

A missing status is not necessarily a measured zero. If the warehouse omits unresolved requests, a normalized stack can show an apparently perfect closure rate even as the unobserved group grows. Reconcile segment counts to the cohort total, expose an unknown state, and reserve a separate no-exposure state when the denominator is zero. A percentage bar for zero eligible requests has no defined composition. Missing-state display should use a label or pattern in addition to color.

Audit every filter

When a dashboard filters by region or week, recompute each segment count from the selected cohort and normalize only after filtering. Do not average prior percentages. Tooltips and exports should include segment count, denominator and percentage; rounded shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1, which is a display effect rather than a data error. Linked selections must update totals and segments together. Test one-bar, zero-cohort and category-absent states before release.

Worked contract

def composition_by_depot(
    counts: dict[str, dict[str, int]], statuses: tuple[str, ...]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, float | None]]]:
    if len(set(statuses)) != len(statuses) or not statuses:
        raise ValueError("statuses must be unique and nonempty")
    result = {}
    for depot, segments in counts.items():
        if set(segments) - set(statuses) or any(value < 0 for value in segments.values()):
            raise ValueError("unknown status or negative count")
        total = sum(segments.values())
        result[depot] = {
            status: (segments.get(status, 0),
                     segments.get(status, 0) / total if total else None)
            for status in statuses
        }
    return result

mix = composition_by_depot(
    {"north": {"closed": 47, "pending": 34},
     "south": {"closed": 470, "pending": 340}},
    ("closed", "pending", "unknown"))
assert mix["north"]["closed"] == (47, 47 / 81)
assert mix["south"]["closed"] == (470, 470 / 810)
assert mix["north"]["unknown"] == (0, 0.0)

Performance and operating cost

For D depots, S declared statuses and M supplied segment values, validation and construction take O(M + DS) expected time and O(DS) output space. Reusing a prebuilt status set removes repeated set construction in a larger implementation. Rendering a normalized bar still needs the absolute counts for labels and audit. The example treats an absent segment as observed zero only under the stated complete-status contract; without that contract, an absent segment must be marked unknown.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-width normalized bars as equal workloads.
  • Dropping unresolved statuses before calculating shares.
  • Changing stack order between weeks and implying a category moved.
  • Averaging percentages instead of adding segment counts first.

Validation drill

Prepare 13 weekly depot bars with different cohort sizes. Show absolute and normalized versions, then remove one status record from a source extract and verify reconciliation fails rather than silently improving a percentage.

title: Treemaps: validate hierarchy and leaf totals before assigning area
summary: Prevent duplicated parent values, unstable tiles and tiny unreadable leaves.
body:
Prevent duplicated parent values, unstable tiles and tiny unreadable leaves.

Area is a sum contract

A treemap divides a rectangle into nested areas proportional to a nonnegative measure. To compare storage used by product teams, assign each leaf one value and derive parent totals from those leaves. If a parent row already contains the total, summing it with its children doubles the area. Validate that every leaf has one parent, that the hierarchy has no cycle, and that the root total agrees with the source. Grain checks protect the basic unit before layout begins.

Labels cannot rescue tiny tiles

A rectangle's area is hard to estimate precisely, and small leaves cannot hold readable text. Use the treemap for broad composition and a sorted table or bar view for exact comparison. Group genuinely small categories into a named remainder only when their combined value and membership are reported. Do not simply omit leaves to make labels fit. Stacked bars often work better when the hierarchy has only one level or exact cross-category comparison matters.

Keep identity across versions

Many tiling algorithms can rearrange rectangles after a small value change. A user comparing two snapshots may see tiles move and mistake movement for a new category. Use stable IDs, a declared sort and a layout method chosen for the comparison task. If two versions must be compared, consider a fixed hierarchy with an accompanying difference bar; do not imply that a tile's new screen position has meaning. Shared-scale panels help only when the same root total basis is explicit.

Separate structure from measure

Zero-value leaves may be valid members of the hierarchy but have no visible area. Missing measures are different: they should be counted and surfaced outside the tiled display. A negative measure cannot be represented as area without a different visual contract. Tooltips should show path, leaf value, parent total and share; keyboard users need an ordered text tree or table. Accessible text can retain the small leaves that the drawing cannot label.

Worked contract

def hierarchy_totals(
    parent_of: dict[str, str | None], leaf_values: dict[str, int]
) -> dict[str, int]:
    internal = {parent for parent in parent_of.values() if parent is not None}
    if set(leaf_values) != set(parent_of) - internal or any(value < 0 for value in leaf_values.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid leaf value")
    if any(parent is not None and parent not in parent_of for parent in parent_of.values()):
        raise ValueError("unknown parent")
    for start in parent_of:
        seen = set()
        node = start
        while node is not None:
            if node in seen:
                raise ValueError("cycle in hierarchy")
            seen.add(node)
            node = parent_of[node]
    totals = {node: 0 for node in parent_of}
    for leaf, value in leaf_values.items():
        node = leaf
        while node is not None:
            totals[node] += value
            node = parent_of[node]
    return totals

tree = {"all": None, "support": "all", "mobile": "support",
        "web": "support", "payments": "all"}
totals = hierarchy_totals(tree, {"mobile": 47, "web": 81, "payments": 31})
assert totals["support"] == 128 and totals["all"] == 159

Performance and operating cost

For V nodes, L leaves and maximum depth H, cycle validation and ancestor accumulation take O((V + L)H) time and O(V + H) space for totals and one ancestor set. A deep or very large hierarchy should validate and sum in one postorder pass, O(V). Production layout adds sorting, tiling and label placement. Every terminal node needs a nonnegative measure for area encoding.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding stored parent totals to leaf values and doubling displayed area.
  • Treating zero-area leaves as nonexistent members.
  • Reading a tile move between snapshots as a change in business structure.
  • Dropping tiny categories without reporting the remainder.

Validation drill

Build a three-level storage hierarchy with 47 leaves. Insert one duplicate parent total, one missing measure and one cycle; reject each before rendering, then compare the resulting treemap with a sorted leaf table.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.

title: Parallel coordinates: make every axis conversion inspectable
summary: Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.
body:
Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.

A polyline is one record

Parallel coordinates display one entity as a line crossing several vertical axes. Its crossings are the entity's values; line slopes between axes are visual connectors, not measured rates of change. Before drawing, name every metric and unit. A route whose five service measures have incompatible units cannot be read honestly on one raw height scale. Scale integrity applies independently to every axis. Put the raw value in a tooltip or adjacent table so a normalized line does not erase the original measurement.

Normalization changes the question

Min-max normalization maps each axis to a shared display interval, but a single extreme entity can compress all others. Fixed policy bounds may be more stable than bounds computed from the current filter. If lower is preferable for one metric, invert its display direction and label that inversion. Never silently reverse an axis just to make good records form a tidy line. Target-oriented KPI charts may be clearer if the decision is only whether a threshold was met. Keep the bounds, direction and unit beside each dimension in exported metadata.

Axis order and brushing are analytic choices

Swapping two adjacent axes changes which relationships are visually easiest to see, even though the data stay unchanged. Pick an order tied to the question, such as intake, response, resolution and cost, then preserve it across comparable views. Brushing one range selects entities; a linked table should show which IDs remain and how many were excluded. Linked filters require explicit cohort state. Avoid drawing every record at full opacity: a thousand crossing lines become an opaque band. Sampling must retain a visible selected count and a full-population summary.

Missing values must not become fabricated paths

A line should break or be omitted with an explicit reason when one dimension is absent; zero is not a replacement for missing. Check whether the missingness is related to the outcome being inspected. If only high-cost projects fail to report quality, excluding incomplete records changes the apparent relationship. An export manifest should name complete-case rules, filter state, axis order, bounds and transformed values. For accessibility, offer a sortable table of the underlying records and a concise summary of which dimensions separate selected groups.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def normalize_profile(profile: dict[str, float | None],
                      axes: dict[str, tuple[float, float, bool]]
                      ) -> dict[str, float | None]:
    if set(profile) != set(axes):
        raise ValueError("profile dimensions must match axis declarations")
    normalized = {}
    for metric, (low, high, lower_is_better) in axes.items():
        value = profile[metric]
        if not all(isfinite(bound) for bound in (low, high)) or high <= low:
            raise ValueError("axis bounds must be finite and ordered")
        if value is None:
            normalized[metric] = None
            continue
        if not isfinite(value) or not low <= value <= high:
            raise ValueError("measurement outside declared axis")
        position = (value - low) / (high - low)
        normalized[metric] = 1 - position if lower_is_better else position
    return normalized

axes = {"response_minutes": (0, 120, True),
        "resolved_percent": (0, 100, False)}
depot_profile = normalize_profile(
    {"response_minutes": 47, "resolved_percent": 81}, axes)
assert round(depot_profile["response_minutes"], 4) == 0.6083
assert depot_profile["resolved_percent"] == 0.81

Performance and operating cost

For D dimensions in one record, normalization takes O(D) time and O(D) output space; N records take O(ND). Rendering N polylines can dominate interaction cost, especially when brushing triggers full redraws. The code rejects values outside policy bounds rather than clipping them invisibly. If clipping is intended, export both raw and displayed values and count clipped records by axis.

Common Mistakes

  • Interpreting connector slope as a real-world rate of change.
  • Recomputing axis bounds after a filter and comparing line heights as if scale stayed fixed.
  • Silently reversing one axis or replacing missing with zero.
  • Drawing all records at full opacity and calling the dense band a cluster.

Validation drill

Compare 59 depots on response time, resolution rate and cost. Publish fixed axis bounds, invert only metrics where lower is better, then brush a subgroup and reconcile its ID count to the table.

title: Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color
summary: Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.
body:
Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.

The matrix has more than coefficients

A correlation cell describes observations shared by two variables. With missing fields, one cell may use 810 records and another 47; identical color saturation hides that difference. Carry a second matrix of pairwise counts and expose it in labels, tooltips or a companion table. A blank pair means insufficient shared records or an undefined statistic, not zero association. Missing-cell rules distinguish these states. Record which rows passed eligibility filters before calculating either matrix.

Choose a missing-data contract

Pairwise deletion uses every available pair but can give each cell a different population. Complete-case deletion holds one population constant but may discard most records and change who remains. State the choice and counts. A constant column has zero variance and no Pearson correlation; mark it undefined. Do not fill its cell with zero merely to complete a square. Dataset grain and join checks should precede calculation so duplicated rows do not inflate confidence.

Order features for the reading task

Alphabetical order is stable and auditable. A domain order groups related measures. Data-driven clustering can reveal blocks, but the clustering method and input matrix become part of the result; changing order between periods makes comparison harder. Fix order for side-by-side charts, or record the exact order for each export. Show a legend centered on zero with identical limits in every panel. Scale integrity prevents a weak coefficient from receiving the same shade as a strong one elsewhere.

Do not infer a mechanism

A large coefficient can arise from shared time trends, repeated entities, selection or a third variable. The matrix is a screen for questions, not proof that changing one field changes another. Confirm striking cells with paired scatter plots, units and source counts; outliers can dominate a linear coefficient. Avoid painting both triangles when space is tight, since the duplicate area adds no information. Dense scatter views help inspect what the matrix compressed. Describe the population and time range beside every matrix.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def pearson_pair(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                 left: str, right: str) -> tuple[float | None, int]:
    pairs = [(record[left], record[right]) for record in records
             if record.get(left) is not None and record.get(right) is not None]
    count = len(pairs)
    if count < 2:
        return None, count
    left_mean = sum(value[0] for value in pairs) / count
    right_mean = sum(value[1] for value in pairs) / count
    cross = sum((x - left_mean) * (y - right_mean) for x, y in pairs)
    left_square = sum((x - left_mean) ** 2 for x, _ in pairs)
    right_square = sum((y - right_mean) ** 2 for _, y in pairs)
    if not left_square or not right_square:
        return None, count
    return cross / sqrt(left_square * right_square), count

shipments = [{"distance": 47, "cost": 81},
             {"distance": 59, "cost": 97},
             {"distance": 71, "cost": 113},
             {"distance": 83, "cost": None}]
coefficient, paired_count = pearson_pair(shipments, "distance", "cost")
assert round(coefficient, 12) == 1 and paired_count == 3

Performance and operating cost

For P fields and N rows, a direct full matrix performs O(P²N) pair work and stores O(P²) coefficients and counts. Columnar execution can lower constant costs, but pairwise coverage still needs explicit accounting. The example returns undefined for insufficient pairs or constant values and does not provide a significance test. A precise coefficient on three shared rows is weak evidence for a broad population claim.

Common Mistakes

  • Showing a coefficient without its pairwise record count.
  • Coloring undefined correlations as zero.
  • Changing row order across comparison periods without notice.
  • Treating a strong correlation as a causal intervention result.

Validation drill

Build a five-field matrix where one field appears in only 47 of 810 records. Show the count matrix beside the coefficient matrix, then compare pairwise and complete-case populations.

title: P charts: account for varying denominators before flagging a rate
summary: Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.
body:
Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.

A rate needs its opportunity count

A p chart follows a proportion such as defective shipments divided by inspected shipments. Forty-seven defects in 470 inspections and 47 in 4,700 do not carry the same sampling uncertainty. Plot the period denominator or put it in a table, and calculate limits from the baseline proportion using each period's sample size. Denominator discipline is the first check. Do not mix units such as orders and line items, or change the defect definition midway through the series.

Freeze the baseline before judging a new point

Choose a stable historical interval and document excluded outages, policy changes and incomplete periods. Pool baseline defects over baseline opportunities for a center line. Calculating a fresh center from every newly flagged point can move the goalposts. A period beyond an approximate three-standard-error limit is a signal to investigate; it does not prove a specific cause. Event annotations should distinguish observed timing from causal evidence. A confirmed process change may justify a new baseline, but record where the old phase ends.

Know the approximation's limits

The simple p-chart formula assumes independent, comparable Bernoulli opportunities and a fairly stable underlying probability. Correlated batches, rare events or extra variation can make the limits misleading. Tiny sample sizes produce wide limits; values must still stay between zero and one. If repeated points reveal more variation than the model allows, investigate the collection process or choose a method suited to overdispersion. Small-sample displays help communicate why a large-looking percentage swing may be weak evidence. A control limit is not a target or a confidence interval for a business decision.

Explain the chart without color

Show the center line, period-specific bounds, actual rate, numerator and denominator in the export. Mark flagged points with shape and text, not red alone. If a late-arriving batch changes a historical numerator, recompute the affected point and disclose the revision. Provisional periods should be clearly separate from finalized ones. An accessible summary can state which periods crossed limits and which lacked enough data, while leaving the causal diagnosis to the investigation.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def p_chart_rows(baseline: list[tuple[int, int]],
                 periods: list[tuple[str, int, int]]
                 ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float, bool]]:
    def valid(defects: int, inspected: int) -> bool:
        return (isinstance(defects, int) and isinstance(inspected, int)
                and inspected > 0 and 0 <= defects <= inspected)
    if not baseline or any(not valid(d, n) for d, n in baseline):
        raise ValueError("baseline requires valid defect counts")
    if any(not label or not valid(d, n) for label, d, n in periods):
        raise ValueError("period counts or labels are invalid")
    center = sum(d for d, _ in baseline) / sum(n for _, n in baseline)
    output = []
    for label, defects, inspected in periods:
        radius = 3 * sqrt(center * (1 - center) / inspected)
        lower, upper = max(0.0, center - radius), min(1.0, center + radius)
        rate = defects / inspected
        output.append((label, rate, lower, upper, rate < lower or rate > upper))
    return output

baseline = [(47, 470), (59, 590), (81, 810)]
signals = p_chart_rows(baseline, [("week-47", 47, 470),
                                  ("week-48", 3, 470)])
assert round(signals[0][1], 4) == 0.1
assert signals[1][-1] is True

Performance and operating cost

For B baseline periods and P plotted periods, this calculation takes O(B+P) time and O(P) output space. The three-standard-error limits are an approximation under an independent binomial model; the code does not test independence, estimate overdispersion or infer a cause. A production pipeline should version the baseline and defect definition, enforce finalized counts, and show denominator size with every point.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing percentages while concealing sharply different sample sizes.
  • Recomputing the baseline after every flagged period.
  • Calling a control limit a business target.
  • Treating a signal as proof of the annotated event's effect.

Validation drill

Track 59 weekly inspection proportions with variable sample sizes. Freeze a baseline, flag points beyond their own limits and investigate a week whose rate is high but denominator is small.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Chart annotations: align events to the right clock without claiming causality
summary: Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.
body:
Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.

An annotation is another dataset

A vertical line on a chart often marks a deployment, policy change or outage. That event has its own timestamp, time zone, scope, source and uncertainty. A release may roll through regions over several hours; drawing one instant across all regions invents precision. Model it as a window or per-region events, then map it to the same clock as the measured series. The time-series clock must be settled before annotations are placed.

Scope must match the measured population

If only one depot received a new workflow, an all-depot annotation can imply that every plotted change followed the intervention. Filter event records by affected site, product and population, and expose the scope in the label. Preserve events outside the visible interval in the export but do not draw them in the viewport. Distinguish a data outage from a true operational incident: both can create a cliff, but only one is a measured outcome. Population contracts determine whether a note belongs on a chart.

Timing does not prove effect

A change in the curve after a marked event may be coincidence, seasonality, a denominator shift or a delayed measurement. Write labels such as 'workflow enabled' rather than 'workflow improved response time' unless a separate analysis supports the latter. If an effect is being estimated, show the design, comparison group and uncertainty elsewhere. Effect-size analysis is distinct from descriptive annotation. Keep the event visible even when the post-event result disappoints expectations.

Avoid collision and preserve provenance

Several events on one day can produce overlapping labels. Group them in a visible list keyed to markers, prioritizing material scope and preserving access to every event. The annotation export should include event ID, earliest and latest time, scope, label and source version. A revised event time should update the chart and its manifest together. Reproducible exports need both series and annotation versions. Test daylight-saving boundaries and a deployment window that straddles the chart's range.

Worked contract

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def visible_events(
    events: list[tuple[str, datetime, datetime, set[str]]],
    view_start: datetime, view_end: datetime, depot_id: str
) -> list[str]:
    if view_start.tzinfo is None or view_end.tzinfo is None or view_start >= view_end:
        raise ValueError("invalid aware view interval")
    selected = []
    for event_id, began, ended, depots in events:
        if not event_id or began.tzinfo is None or ended.tzinfo is None or began >= ended:
            raise ValueError("invalid event interval")
        if depot_id in depots and began < view_end and ended > view_start:
            selected.append(event_id)
    return selected

utc = timezone.utc
window = [("release-47", datetime(2026, 8, 11, 9, tzinfo=utc),
           datetime(2026, 8, 11, 11, tzinfo=utc), {"north"})]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "north") == ["release-47"]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "south") == []

Performance and operating cost

Scanning E events is O(E) time and O(M) output space for M matching IDs. An indexed event store can narrow by time and scope for many dashboards. The example uses half-open display intervals and event windows, so a window ending exactly at the view start is excluded. It does not infer causality or validate whether a deployment reached every unit in its declared scope; those are separate evidence checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a gradual rollout as one global instant.
  • Annotating all depots with an event that affected only one.
  • Writing a causal outcome claim in an event label without a study.
  • Failing to version corrected event times alongside the plotted series.

Validation drill

Annotate a 29-day response-time chart with three region-specific rollouts, one data outage and one event that crosses the visible interval boundary. Verify the right events appear for each region and export their time windows.
